comments.quote_zh: 是对这些动态的极好入门，我会一直把它推荐给经验丰富和缺乏经验的数据建模师与后端开发者
comments.text_zh: 作者 Martin Kleppmann 的演讲“Turning the database inside-out” [0][1] 对这些动态做了极好的入门介绍，我会一直把它推荐给经验丰富和缺乏经验的数据建模师与后端开发者。它很有教学法地梳理了关系数据库里通常做事情的方式，清晰到逐字逐句都算得上我见过的最好的教程之一……但它同时把一条叙事编织起来：“怎样才能做得更好/更具扩展性/更可靠/对业务需求更灵活”，并指向流式/事件溯源架构。你可能未必立刻需要后者，但把它放进你的工具箱是非常棒的，这样你就能说“啊，这个新需求感觉会大大受益于这种架构。”尤其是对刚开始思考消息队列“为什么”的 OP 来说，这可能是极有价值的第一步。[0] [VIDEO] [1] [LINK]
comments.text: The talk on "Turning the database inside-out" [0][1] by the author, Martin Kleppmann, is a fantastic intro to these dynamics, and it's something I'll always recommend to both experienced and inexperienced data modelers and backend developers. It goes pedagogically through the way things are typically done in a relational database in such a clear way that word-for-word it's one of the best tutorials I've seen... but it also weaves a narrative of "how can this be done better/more scalably/more reliably/more flexibly-to-business-needs" in pointing to a streaming/event-sourcing architecture. You may or not need the latter right away, but it's a fantastic tool to have in your toolbox to be able to say "ah, this new requirement feels like it would benefit hugely from this architecture." Especially for OP who's starting to think about the "why" of messaging queues, this could be a fantastically valuable first step. [0] [VIDEO] [1] [LINK]

comments.author: chamomeal
comments.story_title: Replacing a cache service with a database
comments.why_zh: 改变了评论者对缓存和派生数据的看法
comments.quote_zh: 这个关于 Apache Samza 的演讲彻底改变了我对缓存和派生数据的整体看法
comments.text_zh: 不知道，我觉得缓存是很多设计良好的系统里至关重要的一部分。外面有大量非常适合缓存的数据。如果失效事件定义得很清楚，或者数据陈旧一点也没关系（比如周级/月级的仪表盘），那就是用缓存的绝佳理由。我宁愿直接把这些值塞进缓存，也不想去琢磨别的更复杂的方案。我也觉得它就是大型系统里必要的恶。有时候你确实需要派生数据。你甚至可以把数据库看成一种缓存：『真正的』数据是曾经更新过数据库的每一个事件所组成的流！（是的，这是在拉伸 cache 的含义，哈哈）不过我同意，缓存常常是给糟糕架构贴的一块廉价创可贴。这个关于 Apache Samza 的演讲彻底改变了我对缓存和派生数据的整体看法：[视频]。还有这个访谈对超大规模系统（具体说是 Twitter）中缓存面临的问题有一些有趣的洞见：[链接]
comments.text: Idk I think caching is a crucial part of many well-designed systems. There’s a lot of very cache-able data out there. If invalidating events are well defined or the data is fine being stale (week/month level dashboards, for example), that’s a fantastic reason to use a cache. I’d much rather just stuff those values in a cache than figure out any other more complicated solution. I also just think it’s a necessary evil of big systems. Sometimes you need derived data. You can even think about databases as a kind of cache: the “real” data is the stream of every event that ever updated data in the database! (Yes this stretching the meaning of cache lol) However I agree that caching is often an easy bandaid for a bad architecture. This talk on Apache Samza completely changed how I think about caching and derived data in general: [VIDEO] And this interview has some interesting insights on the problems that caching faces at super large scale systems (twitter specifically): [LINK]

comments.author: chamomeal

comments.why_zh: 以事件流为事实来源，得到自动更新的视图
comments.quote_zh: 我很喜欢这个演讲，我觉得你应该看看！
comments.text_zh: 嘿 OP，你可能已经看过了，但万一你没看到我的另一条评论：你绝对应该看看 Martin Kleppman 的这个演讲。[视频] 里面详细讲了 Apache Samza，我没完全搞懂，但它看起来和你这里说的很像。他讲到，如果你本质上可以用事件流而不是数据库作为事实来源，并且有一个足够强大的流处理器，你就可以通过消费流事件来在那份数据上定义视图。最终结果有点像是一个自动更新的缓存，没有失效问题，也没有竞态条件。需要在数据上建个新视图？只要定义它，然后把整个事件流跑一遍。流一旦处理完，那份数据源就永远是准确、最新的。我不是搞数据库的，这些东西大部分都超出我的理解范围，但我很喜欢这个演讲，我觉得你应该看看！我读你的帖子时第一个想到的就是它。
comments.text: Hey OP you may have seen this already, but in case you didn’t see my other comment, you should definitely check out this talk by Martin Kleppman. [VIDEO] It details Apache samza, which I didn’t totally grasp but it seems similar to what you’re talking about here. He talks about how if you could essentially use an event stream as your source of truth instead of a database, and you had a sufficiently powerful stream processor, you could define views on that data by consuming stream events. The end result is kind of like an auto-updating cache with no invalidation issues or race conditions. Need a new view on the data? Just define it and run the entire event stream through it. Once the stream is processed, that source of data is perpetually accurate and up-to-date. I’m not a database guy and most of this stuff is over my head, but I loved this talk and I think you should check it out! It’s the first thing I thought of when I read your post.

comments.author: z1mm32m4n
comments.story_title: Alan Kay on the misunderstanding of OOP (1998)
comments.why_zh: 把流处理作为一种编程架构，并与消息传递联系起来
comments.quote_zh: 我认为这个视频[1]很好地讲述了把流处理作为一种编程架构。
comments.text_zh: 听 Alan Kay 谈论“消息传递”的方式，总会让我想起两种技术：Flux/Redux 架构，以及 Apache Samza 和 Kafka。 > 构建出色且可增长系统的关键，更多在于设计模块之间如何通信，而不是它们内部的属性和行为应该是什么。 用 React 和 Flux 时，情况正是如此！你在定义视图组件，当有人与它们交互时，会触发一组非常有结构、离散的动作。这些动作随后被分发并在别处处理，但在核心某处，对于任意给定消息会发生什么，存在单一事实来源。至于 Apache Samza，我认为这个视频[1]很好地讲述了把流处理作为一种编程架构。处理信息流与处理模块之间的消息之间存在联系，而那个视频在揭示这一点上做得不错。 [1]: [视频] “Turning the database inside out with Apache Samza”
comments.text: Hearing the way Alan Kay talks about "messaging" always reminds me of two technologies: the Flux/Redux architecture and Apache Samza & Kafka. > The key in making great and growable systems is much more to design how its modules communicate rather than what their internal properties and behaviors should be. With React and Flux, this is exactly what's going on! You're defining view components, and when someone interacts with them, there's a very structured, discrete set of actions that can be fired. These actions are then dispatched and handled elsewhere, but somewhere at the core, there's a single source of truth for what happens upon any given message. And for Apache Samza, I think this video[1] does a nice job of talking about stream processing as a programming architecture. There's a connection to be made between processing streams of information and processing messages between modules, and that video goes a good way towards exposing it. [1]: [VIDEO] "Turning the database inside out with Apache Samza"

comments.text_zh: 我完全赞同，因为这事就发生在我身上。我是那种通过自己犯错来学习的人（而不是从别人的错误中学习，那是聪明人做的事）——天哪，我从尝试用事件溯源构建通用目的应用这个错误里学到了太多。理论上，事件溯源是所有应用都应该采用的构建方式。我最初被 Martin Kleppmann 的演讲“Turning the Database Inside Out”（2014）[0] 带入这套方法论。回头看，我觉得自己一直潜意识地感到原地修改状态有点不对劲。你会丢失信息。你会丢失可问责性。毕竟，“会计不用橡皮擦”，而 Martin 的演讲验证了我对数据的许多强迫症式的不安。正如 Charity Majors 在 Twitter 上指出的 [1]：> ……虽然与任何单一优化相比，存储原始事件可能“昂贵”，但所有优化都可以从原始事件派生出来。反过来则不可能。确实如此。表-流对偶性 [2][3] 意味着，如果你存储事件，之后就可以把这些事件投影成适合任何用例的完美表。但如果你把那些事件转换成一个投影并存储那个投影，那么，你存储的表就是你所拥有的数据。你最终只拥有一个聚合。不幸的是，当你尝试存储事件而不是表格数据时，你承担的技术成本是巨大的。出现的问题和疑问基本上无穷无尽。要
comments.text: I second this wholeheartedly because this happened to me. I'm the kind of person who learns by my making my own mistakes (as opposed to learning from others', which is what smart people do)—and boy, did I learn a lot from the mistake of trying to build a general purpose application with event sourcing. Theoretically, event sourcing is the way all applications should be built. I was first taken by this methodology by Martin Kleppmann's talk "Turning the Database Inside Out" (2014)[0]. Looking back, I think I had always subconsciously felt like there was something wrong with mutating state in place. You lose information. You lose accountability. After all, "accountants don't use erasers," and Martin's talk validated many of my obsessive-compulsive insecurities about data. As Charity Majors points out on Twitter [1]: > ...while storing raw events may be "expensive" compared to any single optimization, all optimizations can be derived from raw events. The reverse is impossible. And that's true. The table-stream duality [2][3] means that if you store events, you can later project those events into the exact perfect table for any use-case. But if you transform those events into a projection and store that projection, well, whatever table you store is data you have. You wind up having just an aggregate.
